output.query: Hepatic encephalopathy after HCV SVR cirrhosis — does SVR eliminate HE risk

results.summary: SVR significantly reduces but does not eliminate risk of hepatic decompensation including HE in patients with established cirrhosis. Cirrhosis may partially reverse (Child-Pugh improvement) but portal hypertension may persist. HE risk remains, particularly with additional precipitants (constipation, infection, drugs). Lifelong surveillance and HE prophylaxis may be needed in cirrhotic patients even after SVR.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
SVR12 cures HCV but does not reverse established cirrhosis morphology or portal hypertension — patients remain at HE risk and require ongoing surveillance.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the gut microbiome on which lactulose/rifaximin efficacy depends; this is an under-recognized HE precipitant.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. D. is a 57-year-old woman with HCV-related cirrhosis who achieved sustained virologic response 2 months ago with direct-acting antiviral therapy, presenting at her daughter's insistence with a 3-day history of increasing confusion, word-finding difficulty, and personality change. The daughter noted her mother had been more forgetful, had missed two medication doses this week, was having difficulty balancing her checkbook (which she typically manages perfectly), and had been sleeping 12-14 hours per day. The patient herself minimized symptoms. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. She denied hematemesis or melena. She denied changes in her methadone dose or missed doses. Review of systems was positive for mild abdominal discomfort over the prior week and constipation. Her last bowel movement was 4 days ago. She had been started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) one week ago by her primary care physician for a urinary tract infection.
